lead: Tacticity is the order in which side groups sit along a polymer chain that has stereocentres. A vinyl polymer –[CH₂–CHX]ₙ– has a stereocentre at every second carbon, and each centre can be right- or left-handed. The three ideal orders are all on one side (isotactic), strictly alternating (syndiotactic), and random (atactic). The idea exists because this order changes how chains pack, so it changes crystallinity, stiffness and softening point. It is used when choosing polypropene for a car bumper, a food container or a fibre.
prereq: You need 5.1 for repeat units, and Unit 1 for the tetrahedral carbon.

blocks.text: A vinyl polymer has the repeat unit –[CH₂–CHX]ₙ–. Here n is the number of repeat units, and X is the side group: CH₃ in polypropene, Cl in poly(vinyl chloride), C₆H₅ in polystyrene. Carbon is tetrahedral, so the CHX carbon carries four different groups: H, X, the chain on its left, and the chain on its right. That carbon is a stereocentre.

blocks.where: n is the number of repeat units; X is the side group (CH₃, Cl, C₆H₅); the CHX carbon is the stereocentre.

blocks.text: At the CHX carbon, the fourth group besides H and X is the chain itself, read in one direction or the other. In a real chain the two ends are not the same: different end groups, different lengths, and a different R/S sequence further along. So the two directions count as two different groups, and the CHX carbon has four different groups. In an idealised endless regular chain the two directions are constitutionally identical, which is why some syllabi call this a pseudoasymmetric centre. The argument still holds once end groups and the configurational sequence are counted.

At each stereocentre the side group X can have one of two configurations, often labelled R and S. Changing R to S needs bond breaking. That makes tacticity a configurational property. Rotation about single bonds changes shape but not tacticity; such shapes are conformations.

Not every polymer has this choice. Polyethene, –[CH₂–CH₂]ₙ–, has two H atoms on every carbon, so no carbon carries four different groups. It has no stereocentre and tacticity does not apply to it. Polypropene, –[CH₂–CH(CH₃)]ₙ–, does have stereocentres, so tacticity applies.
The tree in the figure separates the three ideal tacticities. Real chains often sit between them, and a sample is described by fractions, not by one word only.

items: Isotactic: every stereocentre has the same configuration; all X groups lie on one side of the zig-zag chain. The chain can form a helix.
Syndiotactic: the configurations alternate; X groups alternate sides in a regular way.
Atactic: the configurations are random; X groups have no long-range order. The stereocentres still exist.

blocks.text: An isotactic chain can be all R or all S. Both are isotactic because the groups have the same relative orientation. A syndiotactic chain alternates R, S, R, S. An atactic chain has no repeat in this pattern; the side groups look random.

These are ideal limits. A commercial sample may be mostly isotactic with some stereo-errors. Stereo-errors break up the regular packing. Tacticity is a relative description; the absolute R or S label does not change the name.

sections.h3: Dyads, triads and why they matter

blocks.text: A dyad is a pair of neighbouring stereocentres. Write m for a meso dyad: the two centres have the same configuration. Write r for a racemo dyad: they have opposite configurations. A triad is three neighbouring centres. The three triad types are mm, mr and rr. Here mr covers both orders of one m dyad and one r dyad.

blocks.where: m and r are dyad fractions; mm, mr and rr are triad fractions; each fraction is between 0 and 1.

blocks.text: For an ideal isotactic chain, m = 1 and mm = 1. For an ideal syndiotactic chain, r = 1 and rr = 1. For a fully atactic random chain, m = r = 0.50, so mm = 0.25, mr = 0.50 and rr = 0.25. These are probabilities for a random chain, not a measured sample.

Regular chains pack into crystals. Isotactic polypropene can crystallise, so it is stiff and has a useful softening point. Atactic polypropene cannot pack well, so it is softer and stickier. The full property chain is in 5.5. The catalysts that force one tacticity are in 5.4.

figure.caption: The tree separates the three ideal tacticities; isotactic and syndiotactic have long-range order, while atactic does not.

spec.aria: A three-branch tree showing the three ideal tacticities of a vinyl polymer chain.

examples.question: A short vinyl polymer –[CH₂–CHX]ₙ– has 5 stereocentres. (a) How many configurational isomers exist if each centre is free to be R or S? (b) In a fully atactic chain, what dyad and triad fractions are expected?
steps: Each stereocentre has two configurations, R and S.
The centres are independent in this count, so the number of configurational isomers is 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 2⁵.
For a fully atactic chain, the probability of m at a dyad is 0.50 and of r is 0.50.
examples.answer: The chain has 32 configurational isomers; the atactic fractions are m = r = 0.50 and mm = 0.25, mr = 0.50, rr = 0.25.
examples.check:
n = 5
isomers = 2 ** n
p_m = 0.5
p_r = 0.5
mm = p_m * p_m
rr = p_r * p_r
mr = 1.0 - mm - rr
print(isomers)
print(p_m)
print(p_r)
print(mm)
print(mr)
print(rr)

traps: Atactic does not mean 'no stereocentres'. It means the stereocentres exist, but their R/S sequence is random; polyethene is the polymer with no stereocentres.
Isotactic polymer in bulk is not optically active. Equal numbers of right- and left-handed helices usually form, so their optical rotations cancel; do not label the whole sample optically active.
Tacticity is configurational. Rotating a single bond, stretching a chain or dissolving it changes conformation, not tacticity; only bond breaking changes R to S.
For a fully atactic chain, do not write mm = mr = rr = 1/3. Random dyads give m = r = 0.50, so mm = 0.25, mr = 0.50, rr = 0.25.

quiz.q: Define isotactic, syndiotactic and atactic polymers in one line each.
quiz.a: Isotactic: all stereocentres have the same configuration, so X groups lie on one side. Syndiotactic: configurations alternate. Atactic: configurations are random.

quiz.q: Why does polyethene have no tacticity?
quiz.a: Every carbon in polyethene carries two H atoms, so no carbon has four different groups. There is no stereocentre, so there is no tacticity.

quiz.q: A vinyl polymer has 4 stereocentres. How many configurational isomers are possible if each centre is free?
quiz.a: Each centre gives 2 choices. Number = 2⁴ = 16 configurational isomers.

quiz.q: For a fully atactic vinyl polymer, give m, r and the three triad fractions.
A sample has mm = 0.80, mr = 0.15, rr = 0.05. Is it closer to isotactic or atactic? Justify with the dyad picture.
quiz.a: It is closer to isotactic. A high mm fraction means most neighbouring pairs are meso, so most stereocentres have the same configuration. An atactic chain would have mm near 0.25.

quiz.q: State the difference between a configurational isomer and a conformation in a polymer chain.
quiz.a: A configurational isomer needs bond breaking to change, as in R to S at a stereocentre. A conformation changes by rotation about single bonds and needs no bond breaking.

quiz.q: Isotactic polypropene is stiff and crystalline; atactic polypropene is sticky. Explain using chain packing.
quiz.a: Isotactic chains have regular side-group placement, so they pack closely into crystals. Atactic chains have random side-group placement, so they pack poorly and stay amorphous and sticky. The property link is in 5.5.

beyond: Not for the exam. Stereospecific polymerisation is a large industrial topic: metallocene catalysts can make syndiotactic polystyrene, and single-site catalysts tune the fraction of stereo-errors. Modern polymer labs measure tacticity by <sup>13</sup>C NMR using dyads, triads and pentads; the pentad distribution gives a fingerprint of the catalyst. Search for 'metallocene polypropene tacticity' and 'pentad distribution NMR polymer' to go further. The same vocabulary appears in recyclable polyolefin design, where a controlled mix of blocks can balance stiffness and toughness.
